h: A Diwali discount: the Commission has relented, but only halfway
dek: In its 6 November letter the Election Commission gave relief to 4.52 crore voters dropped in seven states, but it has no answer to why the same relief does not apply where the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) is already complete.
by: Anjali Bhardwaj, Amrita Johri, Yogendra Yadav
body: Just before Diwali the Election Commission issued a letter that the writers call a Diwali discount. Sent on 6 November to the chief electoral officers of seven states, the letter gives relief to the 4.52 crore voters whose names had been cut from the draft rolls. Across the country, the number of names cut on grounds of absent, shifted, dead and duplicate (ASDD) is said to be 13.3 crore.

The relief is not small. The deadline for filing the form has been removed, and a form can be given even with a reason for the delay. Those who have changed homes need not fill Form 6 and declare themselves new voters; they can return to the roll by filling an enumeration form with the new address. The homeless are spared the paper chase, since a field check by the booth-level officer (BLO) will be enough.

Two climbdowns are hidden in the fine print. Until now the Commission said there was only one way back for a cut name: fill Form 6 with a false declaration and take a new identity card with a new number. Now it has discovered Rule 21(1) of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, under which an officer can correct a name left out by an inadvertent mistake, and those returning will get their old identity card number. To the writers this makes it clear that the Commission has been bluffing for sixteen months.

This turn did not come by itself. On 28 October, hearing a petition against the Delhi SIR, the Chief Justice's bench said that forcing cut-off people to fill Form 6 was a mistake and a contradiction in the structure of the system. Even so, the Commission issued a clarification on 3 November and stuck to Form 6, saying in effect that the declaration would be false but never mind the case against you. Two days later came this letter. The writers see it as a big moral win for the campaign against SIR.

But there are questions too. Why is the same relief not on offer where SIR is already complete, when Bengaluru had more names cut than Delhi? Elections have already been held on cut rolls in Bihar and Bengal. It is not settled either whether those who did fill Form 6 will get their old numbers back. And the frame is the same as before: the burden of staying on the roll is still on the voter, the practice of presuming a person to be a citizen has been reversed, and the right to vote by descent remains. The writers' last point is clear: with or without a discount, the SIR bargain is unjust and has to be reversed.
nazar: The letter also shows that change comes from pressure on the street. The Supreme Court showed the way, activists pressed hard on the ground, and only then did the Commission accept what the law already said. The people whose names were cut are not a number; they are 13.3 crore citizens, and the largest share of them are those who live on rent, migrate and settle in working-class colonies.

The real test is now outside those seven states. If the Commission does not announce the same relief in Bihar, Bengal and Karnataka too, this letter will remain only a Diwali advertisement, and the democratic account will not be set right until the reason for every cut name comes out in writing.
sawal: Where is the discount for the names already cut?
ref: Rule 21(1)
A rule in the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, under which a registration officer can correct a name left out by an inadvertent mistake and put it back on the roll.
ASDD
The Election Commission's four grounds for cutting a voter's name from the roll: absent, shifted, dead and duplicate. It was on this basis that 13.3 crore names were cut.
ank: dropped from the roll in seven states
names cut across the country on ASDD grounds

h: The Cockroach movement is a revolt against topper rule
dek: For Prannav Dhavan this is not a row over jobs and paper leaks but a revolt against a mould that has long treated merit as a moral licence.
body: Prannav Dhavan writes that it is a mistake to limit the Cockroach movement to jobs and paper leaks. For him it is the revolt of that large part of the country which has been told for decades that it is not a topper, and so has no right to run the country either.

The writer splits this mould into two kinds of citizens. One passes entrance exams, builds institutions, sits in the state and writes policy. The other is taken only as a beneficiary of the first one's hard work, or else as a demographic dividend that turned out useless.

In this order merit works like a hidden condition, like a moral licence. Dhavan says a degree does not only open doors, it also shuts the doors of scrutiny. For an officer accused of small-time extortion, or a professional who survives because of his position, the post itself becomes the defence.

And the institutions that make this merit are themselves stumbling. The writer recalls this summer, when the national medical entrance exam had to be cancelled after a paper leak and the future of more than twenty lakh students was put at stake. Many homes had sold their belongings to pay coaching fees.

So the non-topper now sees not his own failure but the failure of this road. For Dhavan this class rejects both the topper's definition and his political contract. Their fight has no hero and no purity; it makes just one claim, that passing an exam is not a condition for respect.
nazar: This argument gives a name to all those homes that stop seeing themselves as citizens once they are cut from the roll. Those without a degree, those not on the voter list, are now asking by what merit their share in a democracy will be decided.

If the movement carries this question with it, it can become a programme rather than a slogan for workers, farmers, Dalit and Muslim young people. Otherwise this too will turn into an election speech.
sawal: If the topper mould breaks, who will get the government job?
ref: Non-topper
The majority who do not come at the top in competitive exams.
Paper leak
Incidents where the question paper is out in advance and the exam has to be cancelled.

h: From meme to stage: Gen Z has changed the grammar of politics
dek: For Sagarika Ghose the generation that the Cockroach Janata Party and the student-left groups brought onto the street is no party's vote bank now; it is a claim made on its own terms.
body: Sagarika Ghose opens her column with one clear point: it would be a mistake to take what came out of Ramlila Maidan and the sit-ins after it as just one more protest. Mamata Banerjee, who has done street politics for fifty years, thought it worth coming to Delhi to meet Abhijit Dipke of the Cockroach Janata Party and praised Gen Z workers. At opposition protests Neha Bora, a 29-year-old CPI(ML) leader, walked in front with Rahul Gandhi. These two pictures show that the country's democratic politics has found the support of a new, restless generation that no party can ignore.

But Ghose does not treat this energy as a miracle. Her argument is plain: a meme can remove a minister, it cannot win a seat. Fighting an election needs organisation, tickets, booths and patience, and the old parties have all of it. So the young have energy, the parties have structure, and each needs the other.

The numbers point the same way. In 2029 one voter in four will be between eighteen and twenty-nine. The writer gives the example of Tamil Nadu, where this generation's role in deciding the result was visible and a straight-talking Instagram reel outweighed the old Dravidian appeal. In her view parties will now have to accept that the young are not just a crowd but the part that decides.

But the parties' attitude is still old. Indian politics has been a closed club of the elderly, where young leaders were looked at with suspicion and young workers stayed a crowd. Ghose writes that a generation raised on filters can tell a filter at once; leaders on the stage want an audience, not questions.

That is also why boredom with social media politics is fastest in this same generation. When anger born of memes travels from the street to the stage it needs a programme, or it rises like steam and is gone. Organisation is what demands daily work and accountability.

In the end her suggestion is clear: the opposition must make this energy part of tickets, responsibility and a long fight. Until the new voice of the street finds a place in the electoral structure, this wave will keep making a fresh start every season.
nazar: The movement's greatest strength is exactly what the old parties understand least: the anger over unemployment, paper leaks and names cut from the roll. In homes with no steady earning this anger comes to a boil first.

Gen Z politics will last only when Dalit, Muslim, Adivasi (indigenous) and migrant-worker young people get tickets and responsibility. Calling them on stage and counting the crowd would be the next link in the same old grammar that this generation rejects.
sawal: A meme removes a minister, but who will win the booth?
ref: Gen Z
The generation born between 1997 and 2012, now voting in large numbers for the first time.
Ramlila Maidan
The open ground in Delhi where the opposition's big rally was held on 1 November.

h: Young people's anger is not India's story alone
dek: Doraisamy Raja writes that the generation that has come onto the street from Sri Lanka to Nepal is asking one question, and it cannot be controlled with lies.
body: Doraisamy Raja does not see this wave as India's alone. He recalls that in the past few years young people have come onto the street in many countries, with different reasons everywhere but the same question. In Sri Lanka the 2022 revolt came out of anger at fuel and food shortages and corruption. In Bangladesh students came out in 2024 over quotas in government jobs, then the movement spread to unemployment and political exclusion and was met with violent action.

In Nepal protests broke out in 2025 after a ban on social media, and complaints about corruption, nepotism and the lack of opportunity came to the front. In Albania the anger was about corruption; in France about the state of public services, education and prices. The writer says the demands may differ, but students and young people were in front everywhere.

In India, he says, this tradition is not new. The All India Students' Federation, formed in 1936, brought students together in the freedom struggle and its workers died for the country. That struggle itself set the custom that students stand with farmers, workers, women and those left behind.

Raja's real argument is that the machinery of misinformation cannot control a generation that has learned to ask questions. So the Prime Minister will have to answer, whether the question is jobs or names cut from the voter roll.
nazar: This piece reminds us that when power wants to end questions by calling them a conspiracy, the first voices to be pressed down are the weakest. For those without a lawyer, without a network, the street is the only stage left.

If the government keeps putting off young people's demands by calling them a foreign conspiracy, trust will break further among the Muslim, Dalit and Adivasi (indigenous) students who already face discrimination in recruitment and exams.
sawal: If those who ask are called conspirators, who will give the answer?
ref: All India Students' Federation
A students' organisation formed in 1936, linked to the freedom struggle.
Quota movement
The students' revolt in Bangladesh against reservation in government jobs.

h: When a name is cut, a citizen disappears from the democracy
dek: Makarand Paranjape writes about his ninety-three-year-old mother, whose name vanished from the roll and who could not vote in two elections.
body: Makarand Paranjape says a name cut from the roll does not always come back, and a vote lost never returns. For him this matter is bigger than the quarrel over vote theft; the question is not whose charge is right and who should resign.

Then he tells his mother's story. In the 2023 Karnataka assembly election she could not vote because her name was missing from the roll. She was alive, she had not moved house, and she had been a voter for decades. Yet the name was cut.

Paranjape writes that his mother asked the booth officer and appealed to campaigners of both the BJP and the Congress. Everyone promised the name would be added. Nothing happened. She could not vote in the 2024 general election either, and this time no campaigner came to her door, because she did not exist on the voter roll at all.

The writer asks who gave officials the right to make a citizen disappear in silence. In his view the test of election reform should be that no eligible citizen is left outside the democracy. That is not a paperwork fix but a guarantee of citizenship.
For the writer the worst part in such cases is that a citizen never learns who cut the name, on whose order, and who will put it back. This silence is what hollows out a democracy from inside.
nazar: The strength of this piece is its example. In a home with an elderly, ill or unlettered member, a name cut from the roll is not a clerical error but the taking away of a whole family's voice. The same is true of women whose names are tied to a husband's or a father's name.

The real test of reform is not how many names came back but the fact that a person can never find out who cut the name and why. Without accountability every reform is preparation for the next mistake.
sawal: When will the name of the person who cut the name come out?
ref: Booth officer
The local government staffer who looks after voter-roll work.

h: SIR has put everything the Commission stands for at stake
dek: According to the Inquilab editorial, the Commission could not have guessed when it announced SIR that it would become such a large trouble for itself.
body: The Inquilab editorial says that when the Election Commission announced SIR, it probably never thought it would become such a burden for itself. Many controversies rise in the country's public life, a debate runs for some days, charges and counter-charges fly, and then they lose their edge. But this controversy shows no sign of settling.

According to the editorial, the root of the problem is that a person whose name is not on the voter roll, or has a question mark against it, runs into trouble everywhere. If thirteen crore names have been removed from the rolls across the country, then take it that it is the problem of that many people. This is no small matter.

The paper also asks when the courts should have stepped in, at the time of the announcement or when the first reports of names being cut began to come. The editorial says the courts deserve respect and the purpose behind their orders should be understood, but when citizens' names are being cut in large numbers, raising questions is a democratic right too.

So the editorial suggests the Commission should make its process, its numbers and the reasons for its decisions clear, so that public trust returns. Until accountability comes, it says, this debate will rest only on politics and will keep returning before every election.
nazar: From Chhattisgarh to Bihar, the workers and farmers whose names were cut have only one weapon in this debate, their voice. If the Commission put its own numbers before the public, the biggest gain would go to those who cannot summon the courage to face officials.
And if this controversy is set aside as mere election strategy, the first to lose will be the Muslim and Dalit families whose names, once cut, are not restored for years.
sawal: When will the Commission put the account of the cuts before the public?
ref: SIR
The special intensive revision of voter rolls, in which names are checked and cut.

h: There is a right to protest, but it has limits too
dek: The Prabhasakshi editorial argues that if there is a charge of irregularities there is the road to the Commission and the courts; the street cannot take its place.
body: The Prabhasakshi editorial holds that in a democracy the right to protest is as necessary as its limits. If a party believes there have been irregularities in the election process, it has constitutional and legal forums, where it should put its case with facts, evidence and solid argument.

The charge in the piece is that one part of the movement being run in the name of vote theft wants to come onto the street and put pressure on the very system from which it wants a decision. The editorial says this lowers trust in institutions, and the politics of besieging the Election Commission takes attention away from the real problems of the people.

The paper also writes that if the use of the right to protest runs out of control, the first to suffer are those who live on daily earnings, because markets shut and roads jam. The editorial says that a movement shrinking to one party or one leader is not its strength but its weakness.

Instead the editorial suggests that both government and opposition should build a framework for answering questions about the voter roll in writing, in which the reason for every removed name is recorded and every decision can be reviewed. That, it says, is the road that can bring trust back.
nazar: The editorial's worry is in the right place, but its remedy is incomplete. When a poor or Muslim family's name is cut from the roll, what it has is a file at the Commission, a lawyer's fee and a year of waiting; in that situation the street becomes its first and last forum.
Those who speak of limits should also say who will build the framework of accountability. Without that framework, advice only to discipline protest becomes the easy road for power.
sawal: On whom will the condition of limits fall, the charge or the reply?
ref: Constitutional forums
The courts, the Election Commission and parliamentary committees, where election complaints go.

h: The way out of the heat is now bought from your own pocket
dek: Data from Maharashtra to Tamil Nadu show that protection from the climate crisis is no longer a question of official arrangements but of household pockets.
body: In one building in Sangli there has been talk of water shortage since October. The building next door has sunk a borewell 400 feet deep; theirs, at 200 feet, does not meet the need. Resident Vinod Bhosale says that instead of waiting for a crisis they should start preparing a second borewell now. In Maharashtra, water has been cut by ten per cent since 16 October and drought has been declared in 265 tehsils.

A survey of about 1,900 homes in Pune found that where water comes for only a few hours a day, more than 90 per cent of households have to store it. Pumps and tanks take up on average about 27 per cent of a home's total electricity use, and in one-third of homes in Pimpri-Chinchwad this cost turned out to be higher than the water bill. Waiting for the tanker, which usually falls to women and children, is not counted as labour in any account.

The result is not only expense. A family that has managed a tank, a motor and the tanker man's number has a weaker complaint before the municipality. Those who can buy protection stop raising their voice; those who cannot are left with a voice alone. The government keeps a count of tankers sent, not a register of what left household pockets.

In the heat this divide is even clearer. A study of 1,560 workers in farming, construction, brick kilns and salt pans in 11 districts of Tamil Nadu found that those working in greater heat faced about one and a half times the risk of a fall in productivity.

The Lancet Countdown's 2026 report says that between 2016 and 2025 India lost an average of 193 billion potential labour hours a year to heat, and in 2025 the loss was equal to 4.2 per cent of GDP. Official advice on avoiding heat assumes people can stop working, which is not possible for a daily-wage earner.
nazar: The climate debate is still stuck on how much less rain fell. The real question is who pays the price of protection. In India the crisis of heat and water falls on everyone, but those who have a way out through a tank, a motor, a tanker and a cooler feel no hurry to improve the public system. Daily-wage workers, farmers and people in slums are left alone at this very point. Official registers count tankers, not what households spend. In our view climate justice means not only compensation but dependable public service.
sawal: Where does the complaint of the one who can buy a tank get lost?
ref: Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change
An international report published every year that measures the effect of heat on health, work and earnings. The 2026 report mentions the loss of India's labour hours.
Pimpri-Chinchwad
A large industrial and residential area of Pune, where a survey of homes brought out the electricity cost of collecting water.

h: Bengal: attacks on churches, and cases against the victims
dek: For Aakar Patel the attacks on Christians in Bengal are a new map of the same politics seen in other states, where the government looks away and the case is filed against the victim.
body: After the BJP's win in Bengal, attacks on Christians and their churches have begun. Last week a team from Karwan-e-Mohabbat, the organisation led by Harsh Mander, took testimonies from victims across the state. The team's conclusion was that this is a new pattern, that the government is not stopping it but ignoring it, and that it will grow.

The theory of former MP Jawaher Sircar convinces the writer. He says the BJP's ground organisation in the state is weak, so goons are using violence to prove themselves party leaders. The method of the attacks is like that in other states: a mob falls on people gathered for prayer, churches are broken, a cross is smashed somewhere, women are not spared, children are slapped, the hardest blows fall on pastors, goods are looted, and the case is usually filed against the victims.

According to one study there have been 48 attacks since the government was formed in May, and in 33 of them no FIR was filed at all. A pastor beaten in his own home was kept in jail for more than a month on a complaint by the attackers. The writer adds one more thing: bigger churches, such as Kolkata's Catholic community, stayed safe from these mobs. Perhaps because attacking them would cost more, in the country and in the world.

The writer advises Bengalis to avoid illusion. In his view most IPS officers and senior officials have no interest in doing the right thing, and he can recall only two IAS officers who resigned on principle. In his eyes Articles 19 and 25 survive only on paper. This is not news of a few attacks but part of a long process of emptying the Constitution.
nazar: The attacks on Bengal's churches are not a crisis that came out of nowhere. They follow the same formula already used in other states: spread fear first, then have the police file the case against the victim. In a society where a minority's complaint is never even recorded, the promise of equality stays on paper. In our view regret over communal violence is not enough; the bureaucracy must be held to account and the cases against victims withdrawn.
sawal: 48 attacks and 33 without an FIR: from whom should accountability be sought?
ref: Karwan-e-Mohabbat
An organisation led by Harsh Mander that travels to places of communal violence and records victims' testimonies.
Article 25
The article of the Constitution that gives every citizen the right to profess, practise and propagate a religion.

h: 1,065 coffins, 486 from Saudi: who will ask for the account of these deaths
dek: Against the government's silence over the deaths and injuries of Bangladesh's women migrant workers, this editorial demands plain accountability.
body: Saudi Arabia is the biggest destination for Bangladesh's migrant workers, men and women both. A fresh report on women workers who returned from there says that some came back as bodies, and many of those who returned alive are broken in body and mind. Several testimonies are chilling. One woman said she got neither food nor treatment the whole time.

According to an official at BRAC's migration welfare centre, about 90 per cent of the returned women she met reported physical or mental violence, including physical assault, being denied food, excessive work, a ban on talking to family, and having phone and passport taken away.

The account of deaths is worse still. Of the bodies of 1,065 women workers returned between 2017 and 25 October 2026, at least 486 came from Saudi Arabia, and 112 of these deaths were described as suicide. Death certificates made abroad are accepted here without scrutiny, even though a 2023 report recorded families' doubts about the causes of death. Between 2021 and 2025 women filed 2,036 complaints with BMET; 1,969 were shown as settled, but in 2025 compensation could be recovered from only 14 of the 110 agencies found guilty.

The paper's demand is clear. Before a worker is sent, BMET should check the foreign employer, the contract, the wage and the terms of work itself instead of relying on recruiting agencies. Embassies should have strong labour wings, monitored shelters and a twenty-four-hour helpline. Every body that comes back should get an independent post-mortem, and where there is evidence the host country should be asked to answer. The people praised as remittance warriors should have their lives and dignity protected with the same force.
nazar: A large part of Bangladesh's economy rests on the money migrant workers send, and that is also their weakness. Women who go to Saudi for domestic work get neither the law there nor accountability from the agency that sent them. Thousands of women go from India too for domestic work in the Gulf and face the same silence. In our view a migrant worker must be seen as a citizen before being seen as a source of remittances, and the account of that is owed equally by the sending and the receiving country.
sawal: Why is a death certificate accepted without scrutiny?
ref: BMET
Bangladesh's Manpower, Employment and Training Bureau, which oversees the agencies and contracts for workers sent abroad.
Remittance warriors
A popular phrase for migrant workers, because the money they send keeps the country's economy running.

h: Why disaster warnings do not reach them
dek: Before COP31 opens, the writer reminds us that disabled people still exist only on paper in the climate talks.
body: On 31 October there was a reunion of former students of Chittagong's government school for the blind. There the writer met Tayeb Ali. During a big disaster Tayeb's family left him behind, perhaps because they did not know how to get a blind child out. Several in the family died or went missing; Tayeb survived.

But surviving was not the end of the disaster. Floods, storms, salt water and brutal heat keep wrecking his life and earnings every year. In Tayeb's words, he did survive the 1991 cyclone, but since then every day is a running war with nature. A disabled businessman in Chittagong's Patharghata area faces the same. The tide floods his neighbourhood and he cannot get out of the house alone. He says the city stays waterlogged too and people get out on some vehicle or other, but without an accessible road and planning he stays shut indoors.

These stories are not lone cases. In a 2023 survey by the UN disaster risk office, 84 per cent of disabled people said they had no disaster plan of their own, and 86 per cent are outside disaster decisions at community level. On the day COP31 opens in Antalya, that number is worth keeping in mind.

Promises exist on paper. The disability rights convention, the Sendai Framework and the Paris Agreement all mention disabled people. But the gap on the ground is wide. The writer demands real participation of disabled people and their organisations in national climate delegations and planning meetings. Climate finance should be spent on accessible shelters, warning systems and infrastructure, data should be gathered separately for disability, and every institution should answer. His argument is that these people are not only to be rescued; they are part of the solution.
nazar: Disaster planning for disabled people has not moved past paper intentions in India either. That a flood or heat warning reaches them, that a ramp is built for them at the shelter, and that the relief vehicle comes to their door is someone's duty of accountability, not charity. The talk of climate finance at COP31 is half incomplete if it does not reach disabled people. In our view participation means not one chair in the count but a share in the decision.
sawal: Why were 86 per cent of people left outside disaster planning?
ref: Sendai Framework
The UN's framework on reducing disaster risk from 2015 to 2030, which speaks of making planning accessible to all and participatory.
COP31
The 31st round of the climate conference, being held in Antalya, Turkey, from 9 to 20 November 2026.

h: A new argument that questions women's freedom
dek: Reactionary feminists catch the weakness in the promise of sexual freedom, but by calling women's vulnerability a law of nature they also close the road.
body: The sex-positive outlook Western feminism has run on for two decades now feels hollow to many women. Into that empty space has come a current called reactionary feminism, whose best-known names are Britain's Mary Harrington and Louise Perry. They argue that it is wrong to call every kind of sexual morality an enemy of feminism.

Perry's book argues that the culture of casual sex has left women tangled. Once consent was made the only moral measure, there was no room left to talk about harm. The numbers back her up. In a survey by Indiana University, about one woman in three under 24 said her partner had choked her during their last sexual encounter. The same figure was 11 per cent among women aged 25 to 39 and 3 per cent among those above 40. Several young women said in interviews that they had to want it so as not to look boring.

Harrington calls marriage a revolutionary solidarity between two sexes, the smallest unit against the loneliness of the market. She admitted in an interview herself that she smuggled a good deal of Marxism into her argument.

The writer's objection begins here. These writers take the interests of women and men as an eternal clash fixed by biology, which hides the shape of society and the roots of violence. Class analysis is missing from them too. But the writer accepts that the pain they have caught is real and the left should not shut its eyes to it. In her view, if women's freedom has come to mean justifying everything, the right will fill that space. That is, feminism itself will have to find the courage to call some things wrong.
nazar: The debate on women's freedom in India often splits into two camps: an official slogan on one side, and on the other the habit of dismissing anything as Western imitation. The writer's third point matters: a woman must have the right to consent, but if consent alone becomes the answer to everything, who will speak of harm. Yet calling women's vulnerability a law of nature is no way either. In our view protection of consent and law against exploitation have to move together.
sawal: Why did women get loneliness after the freedom to consent?
ref: Reactionary feminism
A current that has risen in the West, which offers conservative solutions such as marriage and sexual restraint in the left's own language of the market and freedom.
Shulamith Firestone
An American radical feminist thinker who argued that women should be seen as a separate sex class.

h: In Lagos a generation wants to live, not just survive
dek: Back from West Africa's rare queer festival, the writer asks why building a safe space has become the last stop.
body: In early October Lagos held a festival called Friends and Neighbours, where the Nigerian organisation Obodo opened its doors to people from all over Africa. Queer festivals are rare in West Africa anyway, and the ones that happen hardly show different kinds of media, film and art.

The festival had workshops on story writing and poetry, films, panels and a drag show. One thread of the debate was that being queer is taken as a Western export, while queer African history from before the colonial period is not remembered at all. Questions were raised about what it would mean to define being queer in one's own language and one's own words, and when asking permission for everything would stop.

Panels discussed relationships across borders, imperial pressure and the tightening grip of those in power. Again and again came the warning that survival must not become another word for compromise. The film When Women Gather brings up the case of Lagos, where queer women, trans and non-binary people make a place for themselves in the city's nights. One character in the film, Doja, said that to hold an event she has to sit and drink with area boys, meaning safety too has to be bought through negotiation.

The writer adds something unsettling. The festival's second day was held at the British Council. The question is why, whenever we want our word to count, the table of a colonial host is needed. In her eyes ordinary queer people without means, disabled queer people and the divisions of colour and class were left out of this debate. She believes that until the demand is for life, not survival, safe spaces will keep being built and nothing will change.
nazar: In most countries the struggle of queer people comes down to one question: when will the law change. The Lagos festival reminds us that a place has to be made before the law changes, and that place is often closed to women, the poor and disabled people. In India too drag and queer art are finding stages, but not the assurance of safety. In our view identity politics alone is not enough; work, housing and freedom from fear belong on the same agenda.
sawal: Why has building a safe space been taken for revolution?
ref: Obodo
A Nigerian queer organisation that held this festival in Lagos.
British Council
Britain's cultural institution; the festival's second day was held there, which the writer questioned as a colonial legacy.

h: Still in jail after bail: the Supreme Court's question
dek: The court said that for prisoners still in jail even after a bail order, getting them out is the state's responsibility.
body: The Supreme Court has told the Uttar Pradesh government to identify prisoners who have been granted bail but are still locked up in jail. The court asked that this be done with the help of District Legal Services Authorities. The court is monitoring its own order of 31 January 2023, which told every state to put a firm arrangement in place for a prisoner's release after bail.

The case came from a petition by Uttar Pradesh lawyer Syed Mohammad Haider Rizvi, who told the court, with data obtained under the Right to Information Act, that the state had not complied with the 2023 order. The state government said that by 29 September, 264 prisoners in 20 district jails had been granted bail. Of them 158 were released and the files of the remaining 106 are pending with the authority.

The lawyer said the state has 75 districts but information was given for only 20, so the real number could be bigger. The court made clear that the direction will also cover prisoners unable to meet the conditions of bail, whether they have their own lawyer or the authority's help.

Uttar Pradesh has the most undertrial prisoners in the country. According to national prison data, of 3,89,910 across the country, 73,491 are in this state. The argument is that a poor prisoner cannot arrange a surety and money, so even a court order stays on paper.
nazar: For a poor prisoner bail is not a paper but a receipt, a surety and a round of offices. The court is saying exactly this: holding a prisoner in jail even after bail is the state's negligence.

The 2023 order is incomplete three years on. The real question is when a state that gives an account of 20 districts will give one for the remaining 55. Until a bail order reaches the door of the jail, all talk of prison reform will stay hollow.
sawal: Why does the bail paper not reach the door of the jail?
ref: DLSA
District Legal Services Authority, which helps poor prisoners with a free lawyer and with bail paperwork.
e-Prison
The online record of jails, to which a bail order should be sent so that the prisoner knows.

h: They did not keep Diwali, because the fight for land and the waterfall is not over
dek: In Rewa villagers did not celebrate the festival in protest against a nuclear power plant, and in the home of Vimla Kol, who was part of the water satyagraha, this was the first Diwali without her.
body: In the Rozhauhi and Sarai Kala areas of Madhya Pradesh's Rewa district, no Diwali lamps were lit this time. Villagers are opposing a proposed 2x220 MW nuclear power plant, described as a project linked to Tata Power. They say that when the question of land, water and coming generations is standing before them, there is no heart for a festival.

The protest has not stayed on paper. Two boring machines of MS Fugro had reached the area for the project's initial survey. Eight boreholes were to be drilled, four of them about a hundred metres deep. Villagers stopped the survey. A meeting on 9 October ended without result, and people also recorded their disagreement with the project in the gram sabha.

Meanwhile the death of Vimla Kol, who was part of the movement, cast a shadow over the village. The family says she was part of the water satyagraha, while the then collector, Narendra Suryavanshi, said she was not at the satyagraha and died after a fall during her daily routine. For her husband Jamuna Kol this was the first Diwali with Vimla not in the house.

The villagers' demand is one: the information on the project's impact should be made public and their objections answered. According to social worker Shivanand Dwivedi the protest is not against any development work but to save water, forest and land. People are firm on the demand to cancel the project and save the Koti waterfall.
nazar: In villages the first step of a big project is often just a survey and the last step is the land changing hands. In Rewa people did what the law lets them do: said no in the gram sabha, stopped the survey, asked questions.

The question is how trust will be built when the administration and the family say different things about the death of an elderly activist. Decisions on big projects do not last without a village's consent, and Rewa is showing this once again.
sawal: If the Koti waterfall dries up, whose home will the power light?
ref: Kol
An Adivasi (indigenous) community of central India whose people farm and work as labour in this area.
Borehole
A deep hole in the ground, made to examine the soil and water.

h: A slap for the man who came with a water complaint, then a written apology
dek: When a video of the assembly deputy speaker slapping a man went viral the victim said nothing had happened; now he says he was threatened into writing it.
body: A video of Tamil Nadu assembly deputy speaker and TVK MLA Ravi Shankar has been going around social media since Diwali day. In it he asks a man which village he is from, then slaps him again and again. The man keeps saying in between that he voted for Vijay.

The victim has been identified as Karthik Kumar, who lives in Tiruchirappalli district. It is said he had gone to the MLA with a complaint about the shortage of drinking water and a pile of garbage in his locality. After the beating he was admitted to the government hospital in Manachanallur.

A few hours after the video went viral another video came, in which Karthik sits beside the MLA and says nothing big happened. According to him there was pushing and shoving because of the crowd and people are blowing it up. Ravi Shankar is seen nodding in agreement to what he says.

Now Karthik says he made that second video out of fear. He alleges the MLA threatened to kill his family and a police officer also pressured him into recording the video at the MLA's house. In other words, the man who took the blows had to say nothing had happened.
nazar: If a man who came to complain is forced within hours to apologise himself, what meaning is left in a complaint? This happened in Tamil Nadu, but the question belongs everywhere.

If the very person an ordinary man goes to with small complaints about garbage and water starts hitting him, and the police are seen standing with that man, the smallest unit of democracy stops working. Accountability begins right here.
sawal: On what fear was the apology written, after a complaint about water?
ref: TVK
Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam, actor Vijay's party, whose MLA is Ravi Shankar.

h: Anganwadi workers' sit-in: an announcement, but no amount
dek: The sit-in continued in Uttarakhand on the seventh day, because the Chief Minister promised a raise from December but did not say the amount.
body: In Uttarakhand the sit-in by Anganwadi (child-care centre) workers, helpers and mini-Anganwadi staff continued on Monday for the seventh day. The women are sitting at Gandhi Park in Dehradun, demanding a higher honorarium and ten lakh rupees on retirement.

The same day Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami announced that the honorarium of Anganwadi workers and helpers will rise from 1 December, but did not say by how much. The workers say the announcement is incomplete without an amount and without a government order.

The demands include a raise of 140 rupees in the daily honorarium. The organisation has also sent the central government a proposal to add 150 rupees a day more. The second demand is a government order for ten lakh rupees on retirement, with no extra condition. The workers have said that until the order comes, the plan to deduct 300 rupees a month from their accounts and the new pension scheme should not be implemented.

The Congress's state unit also supported the sit-in. Abhinav Thapar, the party's state head of the social media department, said the women are sitting on the road even on the day of the state's foundation day. In his view women are honoured not by speeches and big events but by rights and financial security.
nazar: Anganwadi workers are not counted as government employees, so they get an honorarium, not a salary. That is why the same sequence repeats every few years: a memorandum, a rally, a sit-in, and an announcement deferred on assurances.

Children's nutrition and women's health are in these hands. Until the amount and the government order come, this sit-in will not be called off, and the first loss will be in homes where even two square meals are hard to manage.
sawal: When will the Anganwadi centres open, on an announcement with no amount?
ref: Honorarium
An allowance paid to workers on government schemes, which is not counted as a salary.
Government order
A written order from the government, without which an announcement is not treated as in force.

h: 27 deaths, 146 cases: the yearly count of violence against minorities
dek: A report by South Asia Justice Campaign says that more Muslims were killed in 2026 than in any year since 2022.
body: According to the report by South Asia Justice Campaign, at least 27 Muslims were killed in violence in India in 2026, the highest since 2022. The organisation's India Persecution Tracker gives the account for the three months from August to October, in which eight people in six states were killed in action by the state machinery.

Of these, three died of police bullets and five in custody or jail. In the same period eight Muslims were killed in four states in attacks by cow vigilantes and other non-state groups. West Bengal and Uttar Pradesh recorded three deaths each.

The report's biggest worry is Uttar Pradesh, where 103 of the 146 cases in three months were recorded. According to the state police's October figures, of the 316 people killed in encounters since 2017, 110 were Muslims, about 35 per cent, while their share in the population is about 19 per cent.

The tracker says that in these three months at least 118 Muslims were shot in half encounters, of which 105 cases were in Uttar Pradesh. Last month an Associated Press investigation found that of the nearly 650 people the police shot in cow-slaughter cases since 2020, about 93 per cent of those who could be identified were Muslims. On 13 August the Allahabad High Court ordered a federal probe into one such case and wrote that all 23 officers involved had already been given awards for good work.
nazar: This count is for those who put such news aside as rumour. When the state police's own account says that one community's share among those killed in encounters is nearly double its share in the population, it stops being a coincidence.

And when awards go to the very officers against whom the court asks for an inquiry, fear of the law ends. Violence grows in place of fear, and the first to suffer is the neighbourhood where people are afraid to speak.
sawal: Who asked for an inquiry into the 23 officers who got awards?
ref: Half encounter
A police bullet before arrest, usually in the leg, which lets the accused survive.
India Persecution Tracker
The quarterly count of South Asia Justice Campaign, which has recorded cases of violence since 2022.

h: The price of stitching in Bangladesh: 32,000 against four days
dek: In the minimum wage board the workers put a demand of 32,000 taka, and the owners asked for four more days to make their offer.
body: The wage board that fixes the minimum monthly wage for readymade garment workers in Bangladesh met for the second time on Monday. The workers' side proposed a minimum monthly wage of 32,000 taka, and 30,000 taka for new recruits or trainees. The meeting was held at Segunbagicha in the capital Dhaka and lasted three hours.

Speaking for the owners, BGMEA director A.B.M. Shamsuddin said that after the unrest in industrial areas over the past weeks, keeping factories running is their first concern, so they need more time to prepare their proposal. They had asked for seven working days; the board gave four.

Board chairman Syed Azad Subhani said that even if the owners do not put their proposal by the next meeting, the board will sit to decide and will not wait indefinitely. Two decisions were taken unanimously at the meeting: members will visit different kinds of factories in the big industrial areas this week, and a review of international standards will be done by the board's independent member, Professor Masleh Uddin Ahmed.

The board is trying to settle the new wage structure by December and have it in force from December, so that the higher wage reaches workers in the first week of January. Workers' representative Babul Akhtar and the owners' representative both said after the meeting that they expected a decision on time.
nazar: A large part of Bangladesh's economy rests on these workers' stitching, yet at the table where wages are fixed their voice comes last. The owners ask for four more days, and the worker is told to wait a little longer.

This debate is not Bangladesh's alone. The clothes we buy in shops thinking them cheap are paid for out of someone's wage. Until the wage decision is open and comes with a date, the account of cheap clothes is not settled.
sawal: By what account will the raise show up in the first January pay?
ref: Minimum wage board
A tripartite committee of government, owners' and workers' representatives that fixes the minimum wage.
RMG
Readymade garment, the export industry of finished clothes on which Bangladesh's economy rests.

h: Siang dam: 27 villages will go under, and the answer is troops and detention
dek: Adi farmers in Arunachal say talks do not happen at gunpoint, and they will not meet the Chief Minister until those detained are freed.
body: An 11,200 megawatt hydel and flood-control dam is proposed on the Siang river, called SUMP. In Arunachal's Upper Siang district it will affect 27 villages, where mostly Adi, an indigenous community, live. The state calls it the answer to China's dam upstream; villagers fear that both land and river will be gone.

From 14 September people began demanding that the dam's initial survey be stopped. In October four protesters were detained under the Arunachal Unlawful Activities Act. On 23 October the market in Yingkiong stayed shut, the internet was down across the district and the protest turned violent. The police filed eight cases and arrested 26 people.

The action did not stop at protesters. Search warrants were sought against young leaders Otul Jerang and Tajong Talom, their lawyer Sunny Tayeng, and Tongam Rina, deputy editor of the Arunachal Times; journalist bodies called the move against Rina an attack on press freedom. Security forces rose from seven companies by 22 October to ten to twelve by 3 November.

The government sent an invitation for a meeting with the Chief Minister from 5 to 7 November, but the organisations refused. Opek Taku of Geku says peace cannot be discussed at gunpoint. A 300-kilometre foot march by the Adi Galo Welfare Society is under way. The government says 8.05 crore rupees have been distributed to 322 families, but villagers see this as pressure over the survey.

Adi groups argue that the dams of both countries stand in an area sensitive to earthquakes. Thomas Borang, former president of Adi Bane Kebang, asks why the risk is to be doubled by building our own 11,000 megawatt dam when the danger from the dam upstream is known. The petition is to be heard on 10 November.
nazar: The state's argument is that the dam is needed for border security. But that argument was not made by asking the 27 villages whose land, river and graveyard are at stake. Security rising from seven to ten or twelve companies, and the consent papers taken from villages, show that consent here is being treated as a paper formality.

Big dams here are usually built in the name of national interest, and Adivasi farmers pay the price. The Adi people's protest reminds us that detaining citizens in the name of security and sending warrants even to a journalist is no way to build consent.
sawal: Whose consent first, and whose land?
ref: SUMP
Siang Upper Multipurpose Project: the hydel and flood-control dam of about 11,200 megawatt proposed on the Siang river, whose initial survey is being opposed.
Arunachal Unlawful Activities Act
A 2014 state law under which four protesters were detained. Once a case is filed under it, getting bail becomes difficult.

h: Water returned, 24 acres of barren land turned green, but the price fell
dek: In Sandar village in Udaipur people came together to hold back water and install solar pumps. The first crop came, but the price of ridge gourd fell to less than half.
body: Sandar is a village in the Gogunda block of Rajasthan's Udaipur district, and all its more than 160 homes are of the Gameti community, which comes under the Scheduled Tribes. Much of the land here had lain barren for years; now about 24 acres are being farmed for the first time. Gram, mustard and wheat in winter for the home, ridge gourd in summer as a cash crop.

The change came from work done together: 180 walls of loose stones, dams of earth-filled sacks, trenches cut along the slope and napier grass, so that water stays and soil does not wash away. Three earthen dams were built, and one of them held the water of an eight-acre catchment and made 16 acres of barren land fit for farming. Three check dams were repaired and two new ones built.

Solar lift irrigation was installed to take water to the fields, and 26 homes are benefiting from it. The work was begun in 2023 by the non-profit Pradan along with the villagers; the panchayat backed it with a no-objection certificate and a memorandum of understanding. Indigenous preparations such as jeevamrit and neemastra are being used alongside.

The first crop raised hope, then the accounts disappointed. Ridge gourd sold at 25 to 60 rupees a kilo last year and has fallen to 10 to 20 rupees a kilo this year. The cost of fertiliser, labour and seed has gone up, and a cash crop at scale is hard on small plots. So people have kept migrating to the cities, where work found through middlemen brings unpaid wages and cheating.

In Rajasthan groundwater extraction averages 148.77 per cent, meaning about one and a half times as much water is drawn as goes into the ground. In such a situation this small work in Sandar matters a great deal. Villagers are preparing to plant ridge gourd again next time too, though there is no assurance of profit.
nazar: Works that bring water back often end up as success stories in official reports, but Sandar shows that greening barren land is half the fight and holding on in the market is the other half. When the price of ridge gourd halves and fertiliser and labour get dearer, the fruit of the labour does not reach the farmer.

For Adivasi families like the Gametis this is a double blow: shortage of water and the market's indifference. If the government does not add mandis, storage and a price guarantee to water works, every green field will produce one more labourer, not a farmer.
sawal: The water came back, so why not the price of the crop?
ref: Gameti
An Adivasi community living in Udaipur and nearby areas of Rajasthan, which comes under the Scheduled Tribes. All the homes in Sandar village are of this community.
Solar lift irrigation
A pump run on solar panels instead of diesel or electricity, which lifts water from a well or pond below to fields above.

h: Son Beel: the water changed its temper, so the village changed its work
dek: The more than 50,000 people who live off Assam's largest wetland say a home can no longer run on paddy and fish alone.
body: Assam's Son Beel is the state's largest wetland. It spreads in the rains and shrinks in the dry season, and this rise and fall decides the work of the villages around it: fish when the water rises, paddy when it falls. More than 50,000 people in these villages depend directly on this wetland. But erratic rain, silt and pollution have upset the arithmetic of fish and paddy.

Arup Das of Dargarbond gave his answer by changing his farm. After starting with one cow in 2014 he found milk did not bring in money. Now he has 1,200 Nageshwari ducks, 300 Sonali hens that give about 250 eggs a day, and an incubator in which about a thousand chicks hatch every week at a temperature of 37 degrees.

Mixed farming opened several roads to income: eggs, ducklings, fish, and boro paddy, pulses, brinjal and kidney beans on the land that is left. 10 to 12 families and two neighbouring villages have taken up the method too, but the road is not open to everyone. Pulakabh Chaudhary, head of the Krishi Vigyan Kendra, says only five per cent of farmers have diversified like this and only 10 to 15 per cent know about new crops.

Fisherman Maheshwar Das catches fish in the rains by encircling them with nets, which costs him nets, bamboo and labour. Last year disease killed the fish and he did not even recover his cost. So many families now raise ducks and sell them in four months.

A study in December 2025 spoke to 160 households in 16 villages; its conclusion was that to lift people out of floods, hail and falling incomes, all three must improve: more livelihood options, education and housing. The state is planning tourism and floating solar panels at Son Beel, but the new statewide wetland restoration project does not even name it.
nazar: A wetland is often taken for barren or empty land, while the livelihood of 50,000 people comes out of this swamp. Son Beel shows that villagers find the fastest answer to climate change themselves, provided they have land, money and a market.

The Assam government talks of tourism and solar panels, but this wetland has been left out of the restoration plan. That makes it clear that policy still treats water only as a place to earn from, not as a base of life.
sawal: If the swamp dries up, where will the 50,000 people who depend on it go?
ref: Son Beel
The state's largest seasonal wetland, spread across Sribhumi district in Assam, which expands in the rains and shrinks in the dry season. About 50,000 people live directly off it.
Mixed farming
Doing several things in one place, such as farming, fish farming and duck and poultry rearing, so that one failed crop or trade does not sink the whole income.

h: The voter in the middle in UP: ration came, work did not
dek: Newslaundry's ground report meets voters in three parts of Awadh who are not loyal to any party, yet the government's decisions are settled in their homes.
body: Uttar Pradesh votes early next year. For Newslaundry, Srinivasan Jain travels the roads of Mohanlalganj, Sultanpur and Ayodhya in the Awadh region. This is a ground report of about 21 minutes, in which Jain looks not at loyal supporters of any party but at the voters standing in the middle who decide the result: non-Yadav backward castes and non-Jatav Dalits.

Awadh was long a BJP fortress, but in 2024 the party took one of its biggest knocks here. The film hears the reasons for this change not from election speeches but from ordinary people's mouths. In a village in Mohanlalganj, Savitri Devi of the carpenter caste says she will vote for the BJP again; on unemployment her answer is that one should start one's own work, Modi ji is giving ration.

Gyanmati from the same village says her sons work as daily labourers because there is no other work. They got a toilet, they got five kilos of ration, but no job. In a village in Sultanpur, Kusma of the washermen caste says both her sons have gone to Bombay to press clothes, and asks how a household runs on five kilos of ration. Kusma, who once voted for the BSP, now says someone else should come.

Gunja Devi from the same village used to vote for Modi, and now wants a change, because no work gets done without a bribe. Her father, Brahmadeen, trusts no alternative; for him they are all out to fill their pockets. In Ayodhya, despite the Ram temple, the BJP took a big symbolic blow in 2024. Rescue diver Bhagwan Deen Nishad says that after a Gujarati company got the contract, the boatmen's earnings stopped and work came back only after a month-long sit-in. The Nishad community voted for the BJP in 2022, not in 2024; they think the party will lose in 2027 too.

At the Ayodhya bus stand, state transport employees, mostly from upper castes and part of the BJP's base, are still with the party. Conductor Arvind Jaiswal says this is a Hindutva government. But some are also unhappy with the SC-ST law and the UGC's caste-discrimination rules. Driver Harish Singh, who has been in the BJP's youth wing, says no follower of Sanatan Dharma will vote for Modi.

Jain does not declare a result in this film. He only shows that the woman praising the ration has no job in her home, and the son of another home is pressing clothes in the city. The decision of these voters in the middle will set the direction of next year's election.
nazar: In election reporting the ordinary voter often gets lost in piles of numbers. This report shows that schemes like free ration and toilets have reached, but there is no earner in the home. When village boys are going to the city to press clothes, migration along with poverty becomes a reason for a vote.

Dalit and backward-caste voters are seen changing parties, but their complaints are the same: no work, bribes and runaway prices. The lesson for policy makers is that praise for ration and anger at the government can live in the same home, and that pairing will decide the results ahead.
sawal: Ration fills the stomach, so whose share did work fall to?
ref: Non-Yadav OBCs and non-Jatav Dalits
In Uttar Pradesh's vote politics these two groups are seen as a big part of the BJP's backward-Dalit alliance. In 2024 the drifting away of a section of them cost the party.
Awadh
The central region of Uttar Pradesh, taking in districts such as Lucknow, Ayodhya, Sultanpur and Mohanlalganj. It was long a strong BJP fortress.

h: A drowsy woman, and daughters swept into the rubbish: five poems
dek: Five poems by the young Lucknow poet Twinkle Tomar Singh in Sammukh, which record the daily tiredness of women without noise, deep inside.
body: Sammukh has published five poems by the young Lucknow poet Twinkle Tomar Singh. An editorial note says that readers of the old kind may see irony in them, but these poems are the truth of a large society.

The first poem has a woman who catches the bus every day. In the morning she had pulled herself together tight, leaving behind the stove, the vessels and a child stirring in sleep. On the way back, for a few moments, she is not a wife, not a mother, not even an employee, only a tired body. But a jolt of the bus brings her back, and one more shame at falling apart in a public place is added to her account.

In kachra (rubbish) a daughter sweeps the courtyard and makes a heap of waste. The poet reminds us that this same daughter escaped being swept out of the womb, and the bundles in which daughters are tied and taken out are also found in this same rubbish. At a wedding the brother jokingly has them play the very song about carrying the rubbish out of the house.

In sahkarmi striyan (women colleagues) a few free minutes at the office become a ritual of complaints about husband, mother-in-law and officer. In apne hisse ke taare (the stars that are our share) women treat the courtyard itself as a stage and stroke their sorrow to sleep. The last poem is about an Adivasi (indigenous) girl whom the city tells to stay crude and silent.

The voice of these poems is cool, with no scream and no sermon. That coolness is what makes them sharp. The poet keeps the full account of women who fall apart every day and gather themselves every day, without weeping.
nazar: These poems have no outside enemy. The home is the place where a woman has to make her place again every day, and the bus ride is the one time when, for a while, she is no one's wife, mother or employee.

There is no complaint in these poems, only an account. The work that is not seen inside the home is being taken out of someone's body every day, and the right to demand an account of that unseen work should belong to her too.
sawal: Why must a woman ask forgiveness for sleeping on the journey?
ref: Shame
The feeling of embarrassment with oneself in which a person keeps cringing inside, having judged something they did as wrong.
The rubbish song
A joking folk song played at weddings, in which the groom's people tell the cart driver to take the rubbish out of the house.
photo_note: Emperor Muhammad Shah carried in a Palanquin by Ladies. ca.

h: Outside encroachment: the cart is overturned, whose name will the licence be in now?
dek: In Sammukh's new story, three cart vendors in one Mumbai tenement share their defeat and their laughter in equal parts.
body: Sammukh's new story opens in a one-room tenement in Mumbai, where Ramashankar lies face down and the vegetables from his cart are scattered out of burst bundles. Tomatoes are crushed under shoes, there is tyre grease on the brinjals. When he left the market in the morning he had arranged the vegetables neatly, hoping half the stock would sell by noon and he could send money for his mother's treatment.

In the anti-encroachment drive the cart was overturned. Datta Bhau comes into the room with wet bags, then Shakeel carrying a sack of sweet limes. Each has his own loss: seven hundred rupees, the whole vegetable stock, broken glasses, and the juice machine taken away in a vehicle.

The fastest part of the story is where the three give a name to their defeat. Shakeel has no licence; for five years the file has been going from one desk to another, and he says it feels as if they are asking for an identity, not a licence. Ramashankar has a licence and his cart was overturned anyway, because this time the same contractor was with the police.

Sarang Upadhyay does not show these men begging. Cutting onions, Datta Bhau laughs and says the Marathi man got hit too, so what of a bhaiya or a Muslim. Singing a Ganpati Bappa song, Shakeel raises a hand towards the policeman at the signal. Laughter rises in the room and then sinks into the damp of the walls.

The story does not end on some big decision. Next morning all of them have to go to the confiscation office again; fine if the machine is found, and if not, another loan. This is the most honest thing about the story.
nazar: In cities, anti-encroachment drives fall first on those whose papers are not complete, and the road to completing papers is itself a long runaround. The cart of the man whose labour keeps a city's vegetable market going is cleared in a single morning.

In our view the story also reminds us that the person we call an outsider is often a worker from another state. His name, his language and his cart together are the stubbornness of living in one place, and that stubbornness should not be called encroachment.
sawal: The cart is overturned, so which desk will the licence file go to?
ref: Encroachment
In official papers, the occupation of a spot that the administration runs drives to remove, though for a city's poor it is their livelihood and their home.
Confiscation
Action by the administration to take away goods or a cart, to get which back one has to run from office to office.

h: The rope swinging over the well: two people alone even while together
dek: A story by Suman Shekhar in Jankipul, in which every exchange between husband and wife stops halfway for fear of going wrong.
body: Suman Shekhar's story Kuen par jhoolti rassi (the rope swinging over the well) in Jankipul opens on an evening when the husband comes back to the room and tells his wife Ruchi that one day his mother and father will die and he will be the one who has to set fire to their bodies. That is where the talk goes wrong.

The story's real subject is the loneliness that survives inside a marriage too. It has been three and a half years, the two live together, they look happy in photographs, but fear arrives first at every chance to talk. Coming back from work the husband mutters to himself on the road, tries to talk to Ruchi, and every time the talk falls into the same pit.

The sharpest thing is that he tells his wife that when he was very broken he paid women to listen to his fears. He thinks he is being honest; Ruchi feels betrayed. The story does not prove either of them wrong, it only shows both their languages failing.

In between come the thought of his parents' death, the image of a rope hanging over a well, an old man sitting with his legs stretched out in a park and children playing; all of it is an attempt to shake the silence that will not come into words. At the end Ruchi's phone rings and the rope trembles.
The story's turning point is not a reconciliation, only a phone call. But that call does hold this much: the thread is not yet broken, and one of the two has to reach out first.
nazar: We often assume that loneliness inside a home is only old people's problem. This story shows that young couples too can live under one roof like two separate rooms, and that does not need anyone's bad intention.

In our view the biggest lack is that we have no place to speak of fear and brokenness. A man must either stay quiet or pay someone to listen. The story leaves its question right here, and that is why it does not remain only a story about a marriage.
sawal: With the one you love, who will start talking about fear?
ref: Kuen par jhoolti rassi (the rope swinging over the well)

The story brings in a fort's well, where, according to a guide, the king had people no longer fit to live tied to a rope and dropped in. This image becomes the metaphor of fear and escape through the story.
Monologue
The part of a play in which a character speaks to himself, with no one in front to hear.
photo_note: Gaganendranath Tagore - City in the Night, 1925.jpg

h: Yatish Kumar's poem on Bimal De's travel book
dek: Yatish Kumar has read the Bengali travelogue Mahatirtha ke Antim Yatri (the last traveller to the great pilgrimage) as a poem in nine sections.
body: Bimal De's Bengali travelogue Mahatirtha ke Antim Yatri (the last traveller to the great pilgrimage) holds a very high place in Bengali. A few years ago Lokbharati brought out its Hindi translation, done by Dilip Kumar Banerji. Yatish Kumar has written on this book not as a review report but as a poem in nine sections.

The poem calls travel not a pilgrimage or tourism but a way of untying knots. Walking the road matters less than understanding that breaking is not losing every time, and that joy too has to be smashed like a cooking pot.

Mountain, river, fire, snowflakes and salt move together in the poem. Between the mountain's limit and the sky's spread the poet sees the mandala, that inner circle a person has searched for across lifetimes. In the mountains there is poverty but no theft, no locks but trust, and a collective act like fire is found there in its most beautiful form.

The last sections bring in Tibet, where, the poet says, the Mahabharata is still being lived, and where the Himalaya holds both the Buddha and enmity at once. This poem does not preach a religion; it only marks the difference between a truth seen and a truth lived.

Yatish Kumar's language is not that of a travelogue but of a chant, plain and full of repetition. Even those who keep no diary on a journey will read this and recognise the salt-like smell of the road.
nazar: Travel writing in Hindi often ends up as an account of places seen. This poem is different from that habit, because it looks less at climbing a mountain than at what changes inside the one who climbs.

In our view travelogues from Bengali and other Indian languages must come into Hindi. Otherwise we will keep looking at our own country's mountains and people through the glasses of English books, and the loss is not literature's alone.
sawal: Why is a journey not complete without leaving the mountain and coming back?
ref: Mandala
In ancient Indian thought, a circle or ring that the traveller seeks on the inward journey. In the poem the mountain's base itself is called the mandala.
Bimal De
A senior Bengali fiction writer and traveller, whose travelogue has won a high place in Bengali literature.

h: Akhtar Orainvi's story, in which illness becomes a metaphor
dek: An essay on Inquilab's literature page that treats mental solitude as the biggest subject in Orainvi's stories.
body: Inquilab's literature page carries an essay by Professor Sarwar Al-Huda that uses the occasion of re-reading Akhtar Orainvi's stories. Its base is a memorial gathering for Orainvi held in Azamgarh on 14 October, where his story Kaliyan aur Kaante (buds and thorns) was read out.

The essay claims this is the first Urdu story in which illness becomes the story's metaphor. The hospital's atmosphere, the patient lying on the bed, the silence of the sanatorium and the fear of death all step out of life and become the world inside the story. According to the writer, where the story ends is really where it begins.

The writer recalls how Balraj Menra would change colour whenever he mentioned this story. Orainvi wrote himself that when he learned of his illness it was as if a relationship was established with Keats, because Keats too had TB.

The second part of the essay is hard on criticism. According to the writer, for many years critics measured Orainvi only by his social concerns and assumed the artist had forgotten his own self. No attempt was made even to look at his mental solitude.
In Orainvi, social concern and loneliness are not opposites but two banks of the same language. The essay leads towards that dark region which nothing else in life or art can fill.
In that sense this essay is not only a remembrance of a writer. It is also a reminder of the criticism that shrinks from looking into a writer's inner room.
nazar: Hindi readers still know very little of the Urdu short story. Writers like Orainvi often stay folded inside Urdu's own world, while their stories raise the very questions every language's reader faces today.

In our view we still hesitate to accept illness, loneliness and fear as subjects of literature. This essay reminds us that the writer who can turn the darkness inside himself into a story is the one who can also write society's larger truth without dishonesty.
sawal: Why was the loneliness of the writer who made illness a metaphor left unseen?
ref: Akhtar Orainvi
An Urdu fiction writer in whose stories illness, loneliness and the suffocation of middle-class life keep returning.
Mental solitude
That lonely state of the mind in which a person, even in a crowd, cannot tell anyone what he carries.

h: A book on Aligarh: a city beyond Sir Syed
dek: Ateef Sayyad's book does not let Aligarh be limited to the Aligarh movement and the university.
body: Ateef Sayyad's new book on Aligarh, Aligarh: The City That Outlasted Empires, has been reviewed in Scroll by A. M. Gautam. According to the reviewer, the writer wrote this book because he could not find a history of his city that did not circle only around the Aligarh movement and the Muslim university.

The book carries the city from Koil to Aligarh, from Qutbuddin Aibak's attack through the Delhi Sultanate, the Mughals, the Marathas and the British. The scenes of siege are so alive that reading them feels like a play, yet the dates never slip.

What draws the reviewer most is the Koil minar, which no longer exists and which most people in Aligarh do not even know of. The writer is so bound to the city that his regret enters the book's language, and the memory of stones gone by reads like a personal wound.

Sir Syed Ahmed Khan is the book's biggest character, but the writer does not stop at praising him. Citing a hateful remark about an Aligarh labourer printed in the 1868 book The People of India, he shows in what suffocation Sir Syed's work began, and that this suffocation did not fully lift even after independence.

One wish of the reviewer stays unfulfilled: he wanted more on the city's food, speech, art and folk tales. But he admits himself that the book is so large that the reader is left with new questions about his own city.
nazar: We usually know Aligarh by the name of a university and a political movement. The book reminds us that the city is older than both, and that the history of its lanes, artisans and dialects does not end at the name of any one institution.

In our view this is the most necessary point today, when debates over the names and histories of cities are shrinking to slogans. A city's real face is made by the workers, artisans and students who live in it, and their share in history should be equal too.
sawal: Why does a city's history begin only with a college?
ref: Koil
The old name of Aligarh, mentioned in the accounts of Qutbuddin Aibak's attack.
The People of India
A book of photographs and descriptions published in 1868, in which the colonial gaze presented Indians in a demeaning way.
